rows.practice: surveys and measures land and buildings, appraises materials and their decay, quantifies costs and applies planning, procurement and project management techniques to a scheme
rows.knowledge: construction technology, building regulations and the Building Safety Regulator, valuation and market evidence, geospatial science and the legal frameworks of tenure and agency
rows.identity: a surveyor or construction professional in training who applies professional codes and a personal moral compass, protecting clients, communities and the environment

rows.practice: makes well-judged development and investment decisions on incomplete data, running sensitivity analyses on site value and evaluating how buildings perform after occupation
rows.knowledge: how climate change, demographic shift and PropTech reshape property markets and how planning obligations, whole-life carbon and the golden thread of safety information bear on value
rows.identity: a built environment professional who weighs the ethics of cutting fire safety costs through value engineering, owes duties to clients and the public and promotes inclusion across the property cycle

rows.practice: critically evaluates current built environment research and advanced scholarship and produces new insight into land, construction or property practice
rows.knowledge: how research moves knowledge of the built environment forward and where the limits of current theory on land, buildings and markets lie
rows.identity: a self-directed surveying or construction scholar-practitioner who pushes the field's knowledge forward through own professional and academic development (ing's reading)

subjectSpecific.text: By the end of your degree you will be able to show familiarity with a wide range of the subject's facts and principles while aware of where current theory and applied knowledge stop.
By the end of your degree you will be able to understand that the way a problem is defined, and the information around it, is provisional, and leave room for competing explanations in the subject.
By the end of your degree you will be able to show understanding of what defines the subject, gained through in-depth or cross-curricular study or research.

transferable.text: By the end of your degree you will be able to tackle problems by gathering, analysing and judging qualitative and quantitative information, then using it inventively to solve problems, introduce innovations and take decisions through to completion.
By the end of your degree you will be able to plan and carry out research or development work, judge its outcomes, reach sound conclusions and make recommendations.
By the end of your degree you will be able to evaluate and interpret, even-handedly, new information that others supply from a range of fields.
By the end of your degree you will be able to show general scholarly skills and professional skills specific to your award, and the ability to pick up the new competencies a career needs.
By the end of your degree you will be able to recognise the limits of your knowledge and skills and know when, how and where to get authoritative advice.
By the end of your degree you will be able to weigh the effects of human activity on ethics, equality and inclusion, so that communities and the environment can be sustained as well as possible.

statements.appliesTo: graduates of the subject
statements.about: applying EDI and accessibility in professional practice
statements.paraphrase: Graduates are expected to bring professional standards and knowledge to bear in embedding EDI and accessibility at work, answerable to industry and society; they should take EDI into account across a project's life cycle and its effects on diverse end users.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates should leave able to build EDI and accessibility into their professional work and to weigh, across a project's life, how it affects end users from diverse populations.

forBeneficiary.text: You should be able to build equality, diversity, inclusion and accessibility into your work as a professional, and to think through how a project, from start to finish, affects the many different people who will use it.

statements.appliesTo: graduates of the subject
statements.paraphrase: Sustainability means development that does not worsen problems such as climate change while advancing the circular economy, net zero and good governance; graduates should meet this by acting ethically for people, communities and the planet, balancing present and future needs; they are expected to hold to environmental, economic and social values in practice.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates should respond to sustainability challenges through ethical conduct that protects quality of life, communities and the planet, weighing today's environmental, economic and social needs against those of the future, and keep to those values once qualified.

forBeneficiary.text: You should respond to challenges such as climate change by acting ethically and protecting people, communities and the planet, weighing what people need now against what future generations will need, and keep to those values once you are qualified.

statements.about: the SDGs, the HABITAT Agenda and national agendas
statements.paraphrase: Graduates can explore how they might contribute to the UN Sustainable Development Goals and the HABITAT Agenda and their targets; the UK's statement on the SDGs and the agendas of the four nations, with stakeholders such as RICS and CIOB, should also be considered.

forPractitioner.text: Courses should also give attention to the UK's statement on the SDGs and to the four nations' agendas, including those of stakeholders such as RICS and CIOB, while students explore how they could contribute to the UN goals and the HABITAT Agenda.

forBeneficiary.text: You can explore how your work might help meet the UN Sustainable Development Goals and the HABITAT Agenda, and you should also look at how the UK and its four nations, and bodies such as RICS and CIOB, approach them.

forPractitioner.text: Sustainability theory and practice should run through the curriculum and its assessment in a balanced, innovative way; align it with the ESD Guidance outcomes, develop subject and transferable skills evenly, and consider the UNESCO competencies, such as systems thinking and critical reflection.

statements.about: digital tools such as BIM and AI
statements.paraphrase: Information drives the coming Industry 4.0 and 5.0 changes, so courses will use digital tools such as BIM and AI for capturing, handling, storing and sharing data.

forPractitioner.text: The course will give students working use of digital tools such as BIM and AI for gathering, handling, storing and sharing data.

forBeneficiary.text: You will work with digital tools, among them building information modelling and AI, to gather, handle, store and share data.

statements.appliesTo: graduates of the subject
statements.paraphrase: In information management structures and systems, graduates should show competence in handling electronic information and processing data with suitable software and digital systems, use and interpret digital data for decisions, apply standards such as ISO 19650 and tools such as BIM, understand how to organise and manage information and records, and appreciate data protection, security and privacy.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates should be competent with electronic information and data processing software, interpret digital data to support decisions, work to standards such as ISO 19650 with tools such as BIM, organise records digitally and understand data protection and security.

forBeneficiary.text: You should be able to handle electronic information and process data with the right software, use digital data to support decisions, work to standards such as ISO 19650 with tools such as BIM, keep information and records organised and protect data security and privacy.

statements.appliesTo: graduates of the subject
statements.about: use of digital technologies, including AI
statements.paraphrase: In the use of digital technologies, graduates will know and apply relevant tools such as BIM in their field and use IT and digital techniques in key subjects; they should understand how AI can make the project life cycle more efficient, and pursuing better analysis and optimisation of design, construction and use is called a must.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will know and apply digital technologies relevant to their field, such as BIM, and use digital tools in core subjects; they should understand how AI can cut errors and repetitive work across the project life cycle.

forBeneficiary.text: You will know and use the digital technologies of your field, such as BIM, and you should understand how AI can make projects more efficient by reducing errors and taking on repetitive tasks.

statements.about: digital literacies: platforms, ICT and safe use
statements.paraphrase: In digital literacies, graduates should recognise online platforms and their limits for communication and information, use a range of ICT platforms and social media to reach different audiences, and show awareness of legal, safe and ethical use of digital technology and social media.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates should know the limits of online platforms as a channel and a source, communicate through varied ICT platforms and social media to different audiences, and use digital technology lawfully, safely and ethically.

forBeneficiary.text: You should know where online platforms fall short as a way to communicate or find information, use different devices and social media to reach different audiences, and use digital technology safely, ethically and within the law.

forPractitioner.text: The course should be designed so that communication, critical thinking, problem-solving, self-management and data handling, together with teamwork, develop step by step alongside subject competencies.
